content:
This essay was originally a talk at DWeb meetup. It was supposedly about my new project, moss; but I wanted instead to present an open question: what should an internet publisher look like? moss is, to me, an evolving answer to that question, a question that needs many different answers.

The read-write asymmetry of the internet

The question of an internet publisher came up to me when I'm in an existential crisis, which seems quite common now, as we witness how fast coding agents are progressing and how much of the work we used to be proud of can now be automated. Those existential crises often boil down to this: what kind of software is still worth building when an agent can build almost any software in minutes, hours or days?

Interestingly, the bigger problems, the ones that have bugged people for generations, haven't been changed much by coding agents, because they aren't purely technological. And one of those problems is the strange asymmetry between reading and writing on the internet: we all use the internet browser every day; it's everywhere, but we don't have an internet publisher.

It was probably best put by Alan Kay at the early days of both personal computer and the internet. Kay believes that read and write symmetry is not only what a good medium requires, but also what it takes to be literate in the digital age:

The ability to "read" a medium means you can access materials and tools created by others. The ability to "write" in a medium means you can generate materials and tools for others. You must have both to be literate.

— Alan Kay, "User Interface: A Personal View", 1990

But both took off in the other direction, and the asymmetry became Kay's lasting complaint:

For all media, the original intent was "symmetric authoring and consuming". Isn't it crystal clear that this last and most important service is quite lacking in today's computing for the general public?

— Alan Kay, TIME interview, 2013

The original intent of the web included this symmetry. Tim Berners-Lee, who created the World Wide Web, wrote the first browser as both a read machine and a write machine, so that it's easy for people to read the web and also easy to write to it. After the web took off in a different direction, he then focused his effort on bringing back the write part, for example with his project Solid.

Yet the asymmetry is what we live in today. With the progress of generative AI now, the machines are becoming more and more literate, according to Alan Kay's definition. But humans are not, even after so many years.

Open web and the platforms: the timeline

Below is a simplified timeline of how people publish on the internet, and it's a revealing picture. It naturally splits into two routes: you either have your own site, or you publish on someone else's platform.

The platform route, marked in red, is getting easier to use and more powerful, from the early Blogger platform to Medium, Substack and X Articles now. But strictly speaking, they are not the web: they are walled gardens that might or might not allow you to interconnect. What's shown here is the English-speaking world, which is the better case; in the Chinese-speaking world, for example, WeChat, RedNote etc. go much further in blocking you from linking to, and being linked by, external content. These are digital feudal systems, instead of part of the open web.

The independent site route also saw many important advances, all of which became foundations of the digital world. In 2003 the world saw the birth of WordPress, designed to enable people without programming knowledge to have their own independent sites.

Around the same time, Aaron Swartz wrote atx, one of the ideas behind Markdown, which John Gruber released in 2004. At a time when most people wrote HTML directly, Swartz's intention was to write naturally as you would in email, while still being able to express the structures you need in your content. Then in 2008, based on Markdown, we had Jekyll, which let you turn your folder of Markdown files directly into a website, right on your personal computer. Tom Preston-Werner, who wrote Jekyll, said that he was "tired of complicated blogging engines".

Since Jekyll, there has been an explosion of similar tools called static site generators (SSGs). We now have several such tools in each programming language, and countless hosting services to choose from. Most programmers are familiar with them, and the widespread frontend architecture JAMstack is also derived from them.

But this all stayed in the developers' world, and regular people without programming knowledge still did not have many choices. The internet seemed to be moving inevitably towards a feudal system, so much so that a popular essay by Anil Dash in 2012 was titled "The Web We Lost", mourning the open internet that people once thought possible.

The contrast between the two routes is dramatic, and it's upstream of many of the problems we see today, for example our attention being controlled by platforms.

In nature, every ecosystem has to start with the producers, the plants that turn sunlight into sugar; similarly, in the ecosystem of the digital world, the shape of the internet starts with the creators, who turn human experience into works that move people. And when the only option we have is to hand our work to these platforms, the only thing readers can do is to be fed whatever the platforms' algorithms guess and recommend.

The 23-year gap

Many of us have heard about the PHP security bugs found on 21 October, and maybe some of us even needed to patch our servers in an emergency. I was quite surprised to learn that about 70% of websites whose server-side language is known still run on PHP, most of them WordPress sites.

Looking back now, the architecture of WordPress and the CMS (content management system) ecosystem makes little sense. For most personal sites, nothing on the page needs a server; so why run a server you have to patch, one that builds each page when someone visits, when you can build the site as static files on your laptop and host them anywhere? With coding agents, it makes even less sense: when a coding agent can implement any design you have, why would you cram it into the particular shape of this CMS?

Today a regular user still don't have many other open source choices, and, surprisingly, coding agents have not changed that much. There seems to be a 23-year gap after the birth of WordPress, in which a regular user found nothing that can help them gain the digital agency they could have, while the platforms grew into new empires.

What are the options for an independent site today? If you want to edit it visually without code, the simplest way is still WordPress, which comes with the limits of a CMS and a PHP server to maintain. If you are willing to write code, learn a bit of configuration and get comfortable with the terminal, you can have the power and the diversity of SSGs, with tools like Astro and Hugo.

Now we have another option: vibe coding your own site. But even if a regular user is willing to use a coding agent, once she starts thinking about editing her site, she will find herself running in circles. She can then edit and create HTML files directly, which sends her back to the problem that Markdown solved; or she can rely on a coding agent forever to update her site. A better route is to ask the coding agent to build her site with an SSG, but for each update she still needs to write a bit of code, learn a bit of configuration and get comfortable with the terminal.

At this point, I would probably suggest she just use WordPress, with a hosted service.

So we come back to the question from the beginning: what should an internet publisher look like? Can we have a publisher that generates your site on your laptop, publishes the files anywhere, and allows you to edit it visually without having to use a coding agent when you don't want to?

For me, the wishlist is a bit longer. I want the publisher to be able to package any file in my folder, a video, a Jupyter notebook or a web app. I want to be able to change how my site is built and where it is published. I want the interface to help me not only edit the site, but also preview truthfully, check thoroughly, and understand clearly. And I want it to be able to publish to multiple channels, a practice called "POSSE" (Publish on your Own Site, Syndicate Elsewhere), coined by the IndieWeb community.

So moss's interface is one answer to the internet publisher question. It's a first design, and much of it needs improvement. But the basic idea is that we have an editor on the left, and a preview on the right. The editor helps you edit and understand the folder and the Markdown files, while the preview responds instantly to your edits, and allows you to deploy anywhere you want when you are ready, with one click. Above that one click is a list of publication channels, in which you can add an email newsletter, AT Protocol, ActivityPub or the social media platforms.

And the interface is designed to run as a standalone desktop app, as an Obsidian plugin, a VS Code plugin, on your phone, or from your self-hosted server. So it integrates with whatever tool you like to share and edit your files, and however you want to access the preview and publish.

Why is it hard, and meaningful

As coding agents become increasingly good at making software, the bottleneck now is not the features, the portability or the compatibility of different systems. It is the design itself, which has many intrinsic tensions that are hard to solve.

The first pair is high ceiling vs low floor, made famous by Seymour Papert, and since then becoming the goal for many good products. But it is particularly challenging here since webpages are the most versatile and creative medium we have. So the publisher shouldn't limit what you can do with a webpage, but at the same time, someone like my mom who knows little and cares little about technology should be able to publish as easily as on any platform.

Then we have vertical integration vs open system: the former offers convenience and a coherent mental model, while the latter offers choices and an ecosystem. And we have multiplayer vs local-first: the former provides teamwork that creative activities often need; the latter ensures agency and security.

These are tensions that exist in other software as well, and there is now an interesting pattern in these pairs. Everything on the left, high ceiling, vertical integration and multiplayer, seems to be pulled along by capital and the progress of AI: new capabilities we did not have before, packaged in a vertically integrated platform, offering collaboration on their servers so you and your collaborators can all live in them. They get solved more or less automatically, because there are business incentives for it.

But everything on the right has a lot of human value without business incentives. Being usable by an elderly person or someone without technical expertise, the openness that keeps an ecosystem flourishing, the local-first open source software you can hack and modify: this has now become the hard part, the part that will only improve if we work towards it consciously.

These tensions are mostly about the design of the graphical interface, since the mechanisms underneath are relatively simple. And the graphical interface is hugely important: many of the things we in the DWeb community are trying to solve are downstream of it. If someone can make a site easily, she can also easily publish it to IPFS, Hypercore, AT Protocol, ActivityPub and so on. That makes experimenting with and adopting all those innovations much easier. And if we can make publishing online easier, it also helps to solve the problem of copyright, when you can pick your own license instead of accepting platform terms.

Important as it is to us human, interfaces are what the logic, the capital and the scaling laws of AI ignore. I clearly remember a research piece (archived copy) from March, when I started building moss, from a famous VC fund in China, 真格基金. After analyzing the landscape of AI, they concluded that they should no longer invest in companies with an "interface mindset", because agents will be a much bigger economic system than people. To me, it highlights the problem of the capitalist system we have right now: when money is to be made in the agent world, it's not going to be used to improve the human world.

If capital treats people as a means to agent-economy growth, then for us tool makers, it is therefore all the more important to remind ourselves that, as Kant put it, people are ends in themselves; we are ends in ourselves. The design tensions here should be resolved not for efficiency or convenience, but for people to be able to create and express naturally, with agency and choice.

Ivan Illich, who has thought deeply about tools and technology, defined "convivial tools" as "those which give each person who uses them the greatest opportunity to enrich the environment with the fruits of his or her vision". And I think many tool makers, myself included, aspire to make not only profitable tools, but more importantly convivial tools.

As AI becomes more and more creative and literate, humans should be enabled to become more creative and literate as well. And I think that a well-designed internet publisher is an indispensable convivial tool that brings human visions to fruit.
